summary: This note explores the history of Satsuma-age, a fried fish cake from Kagoshima, Japan, through an interview with fourth-generation Chef Hiroshi Sato. It traces the dish's origins as a preservation method for fishermen, its cultural fusion influences, and its evolution since the Meiji Restoration. It also compares Satsuma-age to other dishes with historical roots and presents cooking as a form of historical stewardship.
one_line: Chef Hiroshi Sato of Kagoshima explains the history, cultural fusion, and future of Satsuma-age, framing cooking as historical stewardship.
key_facts: Chef Hiroshi Sato, 72 years old and a fourth-generation chef, met the author on October 3, 2023 at his restaurant overlooking Sakurajima volcano in Kagoshima.
Satsuma-age is an authentic Kagoshima specialty fish cake that is minced fish mixed with salt, formed and fried.
Sato says its roots lie with the Satsuma Domain's period and its contacts with the Ryukyu Kingdom and mainland China.
Satsuma-age was developed by fishermen to preserve their catch without refrigeration; frying extended shelf life and made it portable.
Satsuma-age dates back to the 16th century, when the Satsuma clan ruled the region.
Sato cites September 10th, 1550 as an important date, when techniques from Korean craftsmen who settled after Japanese invasions of Korea merged with traditional Satsuma techniques.
Sato says fish paste molding and frying may have originated from Chinese or Southeast Asian cooking, but its unique identity came from localization with Satsuma palate and produce.
Sweet potatoes were introduced in the 17th century to combat famine and became part of Satsuma-age cuisine.
Satsuma-age preparation changed dramatically during the Meiji Restoration (1868-1912), when Western influence brought new ingredients and tastes.
Sato believes Satsuma-age should evolve while honoring its essence; his great-grandfather would not have used some of his ingredients, yet its soul is unchanged.

The note compares Satsuma-age to Morocco's tagine (Berber culture, 9th century pottery), Neapolitan pizza (tomatoes imported from the Americas in the 16th century), and Eastern European borscht (response to bitter winters).
Sato views culinary masters as curators of history and says 'Cooking connects us to history.'
